events.description: President Obama announces new U.S. strategy for Afghanistan and Pakistan.
Secretary of Defense directs CENTCOM commander to provide multidisciplinary assessment of Afghanistan.
SACEUR and NATO Secretary General issue similar directive for assessment.
COMISAF receives direction from CENTCOM to complete the overall review.
McChrystal submits Initial Assessment to Secretary Gates.
The QST conducts a formal campaign review each winter, after which Mullah Omar announces guidance for the coming year (recurring practice).
Afghan presidential and provincial council elections accompanied by a spike in violence (three to four times average attacks), mainly in south and east.
Afghan elections. Insurgent violence ran at three to four times the average number of attacks, but few effective attacks hit polling centers; the elections were judged a notable achievement.
Efforts to formalize ISAF-ANSF partnership begin
Framework developed and FRAGO issued directing ISAF-ANSF partnering
NATO's North Atlantic Council approved creation of an intermediate three-star command (ISAF Joint Command)
Integrated Civil-Military Campaign Plan signed by Eikenberry and McChrystal
Planned NTM-A initial operational capability
Planned ISAF Joint Command IOC
Planned ISAF Joint Command FOC
ISAF established a CIVCAS Tracking Cell.
ISAF issued a revised Tactical Directive to all troops on the use of lethal force and the avoidance of civilian casualties.
Military Technical Agreement between ISAF and GIRoA, under which ISAF is not required to pay compensation for damage to civilian or governmental property.
Serena Hotel bombing, cited as planned from within the Afghan Corrections System.
Decision to grow the ANP by 4.8K to secure Kabul before the national elections, followed by a further 10K for 14 key provinces.
North Atlantic Council endorsed creation of NATO Training Mission-Afghanistan (NTM-A).
NTM-A scheduled to stand up in mid-September to generate forces and provide institutional training.
Planned start of accelerated ANA growth through over-manning and rapid force generation.
Planned delivery of the first C-27 aircraft to the ANA Air Corps.
COMISAF Commander's Initial Guidance issued.
COMISAF Tactical Directive issued.
Bonn Agreement on provisional arrangements in Afghanistan.
UNSC Resolution 1386 authorizes ISAF deployment for six months.
UNSC Resolution 1510 authorizes expansion of the ISAF mandate beyond Kabul.
UNSC Resolution 1806 extends UNAMA and designates it as IC lead in Afghanistan.
Strategy outlined: first stage gaining initiative, then strategic consolidation over next 12-24 months, then sustained security with ISAF drawdown.

Revised Tactical Directive on protection of civilians issued, cited as a key StratCom tool.

Planned start of a new CSTC-A-managed police trainer contract replacing INL-contracted trainers.

McChrystal's assessment recommends ISAF shift to population-centric COIN, reintegration, and an intermediate operational headquarters.

North Atlantic Council endorsed creation of NATO Training Mission-Afghanistan.
NTM-A scheduled to stand up in mid-September.

Planned start of accelerated ANA growth.

key_claims: McChrystal assesses that the overall situation in Afghanistan is deteriorating and that a resilient, growing insurgency faces ISAF.
The assessment says three regional insurgencies have intersected with local power struggles in a country damaged by 30 years of conflict.
McChrystal argues the objective must be the population, not seizing terrain or destroying insurgent forces.
The assessment says the next 12 months are decisive for gaining the initiative and reversing insurgent momentum.
The proposed strategy has four pillars: ANSF partnering, accountable governance, gaining the initiative, and focusing resources.
McChrystal warns that if the Afghan government falls to the Taliban, Afghanistan could again become a base for terrorism.
The insurgency consists of three loosely coordinated groups ranked by threat: QST, HQN and HiG, with no formal joint command structure.
Senior Afghan insurgent leaders are based in Pakistan and are reportedly aided by elements of the ISI.
HQN's links with al-Qa'ida have grown, and expanded HQN control in Khowst, Paktia and Paktika could let AQAM re-establish safe havens in Afghanistan.
HQN draws resources from Pakistan, Gulf Arab networks and al-Qa'ida, while the QST relies on narcotics and external donors.
The QST runs a shadow government with shadow governors, shari'a courts and an ombudsman, while HQN and HiG have not built competing structures.
GIRoA weakness, corruption and power brokers, together with ISAF errors, create a crisis of confidence that feeds the insurgency.
The Afghan insurgency is clearly supported from Pakistan, where senior insurgent leaders are based and are linked to al Qaeda.
Some elements of Pakistan's ISI reportedly aid the Afghan insurgent groups.
AQAM in Pakistan channel foreign fighters, suicide bombers and technical assistance into Afghanistan.
Growing al Qaeda-HQN links mean expanded HQN control could let AQAM re-establish Afghan safe havens.
Iran's Qods Force reportedly trains fighters for certain Taliban groups.
Despite external support, the insurgency is predominantly Afghan.
The assessment says insurgent influence reaches widely, particularly in the south and east and in select areas of the north and west.
Insurgents appeared to target ISAF and ANSF rather than voters in the 2009 elections.
The assessment proposes three stages: gain the initiative, strategic consolidation, and sustained security.
The assessment holds that the narco- and illicit economy, extortion and corruption undermine GIRoA, and that ISAF must be discerning about corrupt actors.
The assessment says ISAF has been under-resourced and needs more forces, and that without a new strategy the mission should not be resourced.
The assessment lists Pakistan and Iran as external actors whose actions could undermine the mission.
The assessment finds that the OPLAN and OPORD lack clear prioritization and linkage, so the five Regional Commands diverge in emphasis.
The ISAF OPORD lacks clear prioritization and does not link RC operations under a single nationwide strategy.
Narcotics is a significant economic enabler for the insurgency, but ISAF counternarcotics efforts were limited by mandate and national caveats.
Insurgents use winter to reorganize for the fighting season, and ISAF has inadvertently matched their cycle; winter 2009 offers a chance to break it.
Pakistani military operations in the border area are an external event influencing the insurgency's operational cycle.
Insurgents have effectively used the information environment to undermine ISAF and GIROA credibility.
Unity of command is hampered by varying national ORBATTOA reports and Title X-funded non-NATO contingents.
Insurgents use the Afghan Corrections System as a sanctuary and base to radicalize inmates and to plan attacks such as the Serena Hotel bombing.
Taliban and Al Qaeda insurgents make up more than 2,500 of the 14,500 inmates in Afghan prisons.
Multiple national prison facilities are described as firmly under Taliban control.
Productive interrogation and intelligence collection at Bagram have been reduced by lack of capacity, and hundreds are held without charge.
Most civilian casualties are caused by insurgents, but the Afghan people hold ISAF to a higher standard.
StratCom should be embedded in operations and aimed at the Afghan population's trust in GIRoA and ISAF.
Taliban and Al Qaeda insurgents number over 2,500 of the 14,500 inmates in the Afghan Corrections System, which is overcrowded and acts as a radicalization incubator.
Insurgents use Afghan prisons as a sanctuary and operating base, citing the Serena Hotel bombing and assassinations as examples.
Multiple Afghan national prison facilities are firmly under Taliban control.
Lack of capacity at the US-run Bagram facility has reduced productive interrogation and left hundreds held without charge.
USFOR-A proposes a CJIATF of about 120 personnel to run US detention and reform the Afghan Central Prisons Directorate, aiming at turnover to the Afghan government.
The ANSF should grow to 400k (240k ANA, 160k ANP), with ANA growth to 134k brought forward to October 2010.
NTM-A, endorsed 12 June 2009, will take over institutional training while the ISAF Joint Command takes over developing the fielded ANSF.
